question: Let $f:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}$ be defined by $f(x)=[x]$, where $[x]$ denotes the greatest integer less than or equal to $x$. Examine whether $f$ is one-one and onto, giving complete mathematical justification.
explanation:
Verification of one-one property
For a function to be one-one, distinct elements of the domain must have distinct images. Consider $x_1=\frac{6}{5}$ and $x_2=\frac{9}{5}$. Clearly, $$\frac{6}{5}\neq\frac{9}{5}$$ but $$f\left(\frac{6}{5}\right)=1\quad\text{and}\quad f\left(\frac{9}{5}\right)=1$$ Thus, two distinct real numbers have the same image. Therefore, $f$ is not one-one.

Verification of onto property
The value $[x]$ is always an integer for every $x\in\mathbb{R}$. Consider $\frac{1}{2}\in\mathbb{R}$ in the co-domain. There is no $x\in\mathbb{R}$ such that $$[x]=\frac{1}{2}$$ because the greatest integer function takes only integral values. Hence, $\frac{1}{2}$ has no pre-image under $f$, so $f$ is not onto.

Final Result
The greatest integer function $f:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}$ is neither one-one nor onto.

options.A: $f$ is one-one and onto because every real number has a unique greatest integer.
options.B: $f$ is one-one but not onto because its range is $\mathbb{Z}$ rather than $\mathbb{R}$.
options.C: $f$ is neither one-one nor onto because distinct real numbers can have the same greatest integer, and non-integral real numbers have no pre-image.
options.D: $f$ is onto but not one-one because every real number is the greatest integer of some real input.
